title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 7: A Unique Mode of Nurturing Democracy
keywords: A Unique Mode of Nurturing Democracy
World Association of Public Opinion Research (WAPOR)
ABS-CBN Broadcasting Corporation v. Commission on Elections
Singapore, Mexico, India, Canada, United Kingdom, South Africa and France
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's address to the Fourth Asian Regional Conference of the World Association of Public Opinion Research, arguing that in the Philippines opinion polling and the publication of its results are part of free expression and 'constitutionally protected as a unique mode of nurturing democracy.'

A comparative survey of how countries treat election polls -- bans in Singapore and Mexico, judicial protection in India and Canada, voluntary restraint in the United Kingdom, and a liberalizing trend in South Africa and France -- together with evidence that embargoes are evaded through foreign websites.

The two landmark Decisions: ABS-CBN v. Comelec (January 28, 2000), which he wrote, striking down the ban on exit polls as speculative and untenable, and Social Weather Stations v. Comelec (May 5, 2001), voiding the Fair Elections Act's pre-election survey embargo as prior restraint beyond Comelec's powers and an unreasonable regulation under the O'Brien test.

The Court's own relationship to public opinion: it decides 'with cold impartiality on the basis of the law and the facts' and resists mobs, lobbies and the other branches, yet it knows it 'can be effective only as long as it retains the long-term support of the public,' which is why SWS surveys of public perception pushed it toward transparency and accountability.
sub_topics: He opens with the joke about a lawyer-friend told by his surgeon that nine of ten patients die on the operating table and that, since nine had already died, 'you will surely live' -- a 'bizarre way' of beginning a talk on polling before the world's experts.

He thanks Dr. Mahar Mangahas for the invitation and greets WAPOR president Kathleen Francovic, polling director of CBS News, noting the conference met in the middle of a full-blown Philippine electoral campaign.

Polling began as a marketing research tool for usage, attitude and image studies, but in the hands of competent organizations like SWS has become a credible index of voter preference -- so accurate that 'one wag naughtily suggested the abolition of expensive elections' in favor of surveys.

Comparative law: Singapore bans election surveys and exit polls; Mexico makes it a criminal offense to release a predictive poll within eight days of an election; India's Supreme Court dismissed a petition to ban pre-election and exit poll publication; Canada's Supreme Court held such restriction unconstitutional in 1998; and Britain relies on voluntary restraint on election day.

The liberalizing trend: South Africa moved from a six-week release blackout to publication up to the day before the election, and France cut its embargo from seven days to one; meanwhile 35 percent of those surveyed in embargo countries said they would use the Internet to evade the restriction.

ABS-CBN v. Comelec: the poll body restrained SWS from conducting exit polls in the 1998 presidential elections and the network from broadcasting results, claiming exit polls posed 'a clear and present danger of destroying the credibility and integrity of the electoral process.'

The Court's answer was a firm 'No': the arguments were speculative -- interviewees were selected at random so results would be representative, the results were not meant to replace the official Comelec count, and the election's own credibility was a separate exercise not at stake.

He restates the free-expression doctrine: freedom of expression is a preferred right above substantive economic freedom, free speech is 'an indispensable condition for nearly every other form of freedom,' and free speech includes the right to inform and be informed and to unhampered reportage.

Free expression assures responsive government under the republican principle, secures individual self-fulfillment and participation in decision-making, and commits the polity to debates that are 'uninhibited, robust and wide open' -- encompassing, after Holmes, 'the thought we hate.'

He adds a caution that while all poll organizations equally enjoy the right to publicize their surveys, 'they do not enjoy equal public credibility,' just as newspapers and broadcasters do not enjoy the same public acceptability.

Social Weather Stations v. Comelec: SWS and the Manila Standard challenged Section 5.4 of RA 9006, which banned publishing surveys fifteen days before an election for national candidates and seven for local ones; the Court held the embargo an unconstitutional abridgement -- prior restraint, beyond Comelec's enumerated powers, and an unreasonable regulation under United States v. O'Brien.

He presses the point with a question: if free expression is guaranteed to journalists and broadcasters so they may disseminate their own opinions, why should polls reflecting the views of the general population be banned?

Limitations: like any right, polling may be regulated to safeguard rather than stifle it -- the Court's own recommendations included designated exit-poll areas, only professional survey groups, distance from voting centers and distinctive clothing, plus public education on 'margin of error,' 'sample size' and 'demographics of respondents,' and transparency of methodology.

SWS surveys of the Supreme Court: SWS has polled public perception of major government offices since 1985, and the Court, sensitive to how it is perceived, still insists cases are won 'because of reasoned argument flowing from legal principles and precedents,' resisting intrusions, lobbies and threats -- 'Fiat justitia ruat coelum.'

Yet the Court knows it cannot command the military, the police or 'the raging mob' and has no money for patronage, so without public support it becomes useless; distinguishing passing emotion from long-term trust, he holds that 'its real strength lies not in its might, but in its being right.'

The resulting reforms: a Public Information Office, an Internet homepage, more reader-friendly decisions, regular dialogues with sectors of society, rapport with media, strict ethical standards, and public information made a cornerstone of the judicial reform program.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' records CJP's address to the Fourth Asian Regional Conference of the World Association of Public Opinion Research, opened with a joke about a surgeon who assured a patient he would survive because nine of his last ten patients had already died. Thanking Mahar Mangahas and greeting WAPOR president Kathleen Francovic, he observed that polling had grown from a marketing research tool into a credible index of voter preference in the hands of organizations like Social Weather Stations, believed by Filipinos sometimes more than the official count. He surveyed how other countries treat election polls -- bans in Singapore and Mexico, judicial protection in India and Canada, voluntary restraint in Britain, and liberalization in South Africa and France -- noting that embargoes are evaded through foreign websites. He then explained two landmark Decisions. In ABS-CBN v. Comelec, which he wrote, the Court rejected as speculative Comelec's claim that exit polls posed a clear and present danger to the electoral process, holding that respondents were randomly chosen, that results were not meant to replace the official count, and that exit polls formed part of free expression. In Social Weather Stations v. Comelec, the Court voided Section 5.4 of the Fair Elections Act as prior restraint, beyond Comelec's powers, and an unreasonable regulation under United States v. O'Brien. He restated the doctrine that free speech is an indispensable condition of other freedoms and that debate should be uninhibited, robust and wide open, encompassing the thought we hate, while conceding that polling may be regulated to safeguard it through designated areas, professional pollsters and disclosure of margin of error and methodology. He closed on the Court's own standing: it decides with cold impartiality and resists mobs and lobbies, yet commanding neither army nor money it needs residual public trust, its real strength lying not in its might but in its being right -- which is why SWS surveys prompted its transparency reforms.
